title: CNBC – Is there an entry-level AI usage paradox?
summary: Recapping CNBC's 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit and discussions around AI agents, cybersecurity, AI costs and business implications
body_markdown:
Nigel Vaz, Publicis Sapient CEO, speaks with CNBC's Jon Fortt at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026.


CNBC


At a defining moment for business and technology, artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations operate — and introducing new complexities for the leaders responsible for what comes next.


So how are companies adapting and shaping technology's next era — from compute ROI and cybersecurity to regulation and quantum computing?


CNBC convened technology executives, industry experts, and CNBC journalists at the annual Technology Executive Council Summit in New York on October 28, 2026 to discuss the increasingly central role that technology leaders are playing in this transformation.


The TEC Summit is an exclusive event for members; learn more about the TEC and apply for membership at[www.cnbccouncils.com/tec](http://www.cnbccouncils.com/tec) *.*


**Highlights from the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit:**


- Where thedebate on AI costs is currently at within companies
- Are AI agents and human employeescoworkers ?

## How CNBC Technology Executive Council members are navigating enterprise AI use


During the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit, we asked Council members for their thoughts on the challenges and opportunities of enterprise AI adoption. Some of their answers are as follows:


***As companies move from AI experimentation to wider deployment, what has been the biggest challenge in proving its value?***


"As AI comes into the enterprise, I liken this to back in the early 2000s when you could get all this bandwidth at your home, but when you went to work, your Internet actually was terrible because your enterprise had to pay for a T1. I think we're in kind of that same environment now where on the personal side, these models are doing so much and these bots are doing so much for us, but on the enterprise side, we're all still trying to figure out what to do with these massive models.


I heard this the other day at another event I was at, that we're all like first-time shoppers at Costco, and we're buying everything now. Now, we're smart enough to go into Costco and just get what we need for the list and buy nothing else. I think that's where enterprise is starting to come to now. I think we're going to end up in a world where we have a lot of open source or open-weight models that we deploy within our environment for the best use."


— *Ed Fox, MetTel Chief Technology Officer*


***What's one piece of advice you'd give a technology leader trying to balance innovation, security and business priorities?***


"On the surface, it seems like security, privacy, governance and innovation are at odds with one another, but in fact, they're complementary. And if you care for security controls, understanding your data up front, you will go faster. You will innovate more because you'll be doing it with confidence, knowing that you have the guardrails to keep your company safe."


— *Allegra Driscoll, Bread Financial Chief Technology Officer*


***What technology trend would you say is having the biggest impact on your organization right now?***


"It's finding the sweet spot between the workforce, your people, and AI models and AI features. We're currently working through having more agentic engineering, so having our developers not only work with AI as a co-pilot, but also having AI agents that can actually do things just like developers would, and then having humans in the loop and training our teams on how to review the work that AI does to make sure we're deploying the right things to production."


— *Joshua Dariya, Quility Insurance Vice President, Data Products*


"We're all searching for the ROI of AI. Clearly there's so much that you can do. And as technologists, we always look for the art of the possible. What's possible with the technology? But how does that really improve the bottom line for the company? How does it improve the top line?


I think we're all working through that hype cycle of everybody got really excited about AI and applied it to all use cases, and now there's a bit of trying to understand the real return on investment. I see real use cases emerging that make a lot of sense. Now we're starting to figure out the cost models of using AI versus people or with people. So I think we're finding new ways of working and really driving true value with AI."


— *Sal Visca, Vertex Chief Technology Officer*


***What's one piece of advice you'd give a tech company trying balance innovation, security, and business priorities?***


"Follow the 70/20/10 rule. So, 70% of your time should be with the bets that you already know and you're going to get something out of; 20% is things that will potentially pay off for about a year to two, and then the 10% are your moonshots. So keeping that kind of a framework to help make sure that you're focused on the right things, and you're not doing that upside down."


— *Jacob Pat, Lovesac Chief Technology and Digital Transformation Officer*

## Who has the right to govern Mars or the Moon?


Kelly Weinersmith, author of "A City on Mars," speaks with CNBC's Morgan Brennan at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026


CNBC


Multiple companies, billionaires and nations are all in a race to reach the next phase of space exploration, much of which is focused on the idea of colonizing, or at least setting up permanent bases, beyond Earth.


But what sort of rules would govern those off-planet efforts?


Kelly Weinersmith, author of the 2023 book *A City on Mars,* told CNBC's Morgan Brennan at the 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit that as it relates to Mars, the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, created by the United Nations, is the foundation of international space law.


That treaty states that outer space and all celestial bodies must be used exclusively for peaceful purposes, and that they cannot be claimed or owned by any nation through sovereignty, use, occupation or other means. The treaty also established the right of all nations to freely explore and use outer space.


"When the U.S. landed on the moon and we put up our American flag, we weren't saying this belongs to us; we were just having a patriotic moment," Weinersmith said.


However, it does raise the question of how can you extract and sell resources in space if you can't claim any of the land that you're either mining or living on?


Weinersmith said the 2020 Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles established by NASA, the U.S. State Department and seven other nations including Canada, Japan and the U.K., specified that the interpretation of that UN treaty was that "you don't need to have sovereignty to extract and sell resources."


While Weinersmith noted other countries have since agreed to the Artemis Accords, that group does not include China or Russia.


"What we've got seems to be the setup for a scramble for territory on the moon," she said.


*— Ian Thomas*

## The problem with Elon Musk's plan to have people live on Mars by 2055


watch now


VIDEO


5:19


05:19


The hurdles that still stand in the way of putting people on Mars


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


**


Elon Musk has long set his sights on putting humans on Mars, and now he has an additional financial incentive to make it happen: his[recently disclosed SpaceX CEO performance incentive plan](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026042639/spaceexplorationtechnologi.htm#id286866c4c474ba490d6531a57db9e93_666) has an award agreement centered on "establishing a permanent human colony on Mars with at least one million inhabitants," a milestone that is tied to Musk receiving upwards of 1.3 billion shares of the company.


Musk has stated that humans will live on Mars by 2055, but Kelly Weinersmith, author of the 2023 book *A City on Mars,* told CNBC's Morgan Brennan at the 2026 Technology Executive Council Summit that even if a Mars colony happens in our lifetime, "it might be catastrophic."


"One of the arguments we make in the book is that it will probably take about that long just for us to make sure that human bodies could survive on Mars and that women could survive pregnancy and labor on Mars," she said. "While we have about 50 years' worth of data about human bodies in space, we don't actually have a lot of data that's relevant to Mars or relevant to reproduction."


"I think we should slow down," Weinersmith said.


Weinersmith said that while NASA has long been compiling data about what happens to astronauts' bodies while they spend time in space, there are obvious limitations to that data set. On top of that, the implications of Mars' gravity and other factors on human bodies is far from understood.


"The data suggests there's plenty of reasons to worry, and I'm not seeing a lot of investment to do the kind of experiments we would need to know," she said. "I don't know if there's enough money going towards that that we will have all the answers we need in the next 20 to 30 years because biology experiments are notoriously slow."

## The governance steps to rein in AI agents


Daniel Dobrygowski, Sophos Global Counsel, AI and Cybersecurity, speaks at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026


CNBC


The situation that led XMTP Labs CEO Shane Mac to have an AI agent post his financial information on a company Slack channel may be a story he laughs about now, but it's also a reflection of just how things can go wrong with AI agents.


"It shows just how many decisions you need to make right in order for agents to do the right thing and not end up seeming like they're going rogue," Daniel Dobrygowski, Sophos Global Counsel, AI and Cybersecurity, told CNBC's Jon Fortt at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit.


Dobrygowski said he doesn't consider what Mac's AI agent did to be going rogue. In fact, he said, this is a situation of "not setting up the guardrails properly."


"It might be a little mistake. It might be ambiguous instruction," he said. "But you don't have that kind of runway to make those mistakes if you're in a regulated industry, so you have to get those decisions right at the beginning."


Carving out those guardrails is a critical part of making sure AI agents, and other forms of AI automation, "can move forward and do useful things, but not veer off and end up causing problems," Dobrygowski said.


Dobrygowski offered TEC members a few governance tips:


Define what the parameters are


Take that a step further and define what can and won't mean


Think about what can go wrong, and plan for what the worst thing that can happen is


"This is where governance needs strategy," he said. "What are you using this technology for? What is it good for? You need to make a decision about that, and that's where you have the trade-offs between what is the safest, what is the most viable, and what makes the most sense."

How an AI agent posted a CEO's bank details in a company Slack channel


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


Shane Mac, CEO of the software developer XMTP Labs, had been using AI agents to perform tasks both for his personal and professional life.


What he didn't expect to happen was for one of the agents to post his bank account information in a company Slack channel.


Mac said that one day, he received a screenshot from the company's head of product of a Slack message that detailed all of Mac's financial information posted by an AI agent.


But, while concerns over AI agents going rogue have grown, Mac said this situation was a case of thinking "it was doing what it thought it should do."


"Everybody loves the train wreck," Mac told CNBC's Jon Fortt. "I'm only here because I crashed the train."

## The 'Black October' cybersecurity crisis will likely compound: Cisco's Jeetu Patel


Cisco President & Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel speaks at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026


CNBC


AI agents are intelligent and resourceful, but they lack fear of consequences, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel told CNBC contributor Alex Kantrowitz at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit.


Kantrowitz asked Patel about "Black October," which is the name the security community has given to the amount of cybersecurity vulnerabilities found over the past month.


"I think firstly, you won't just have a 'Black October.' You're going to have a 'Black November.' You're going to have a 'Black December' because it's just going to continue to keep compounding," Patel told Kantrowitz.


It's going to get progressively harder, Patel said, to distinguish between an adversarial attack on an agent from a bad actor or an agent exercising poor judgment.


"Your security telemetry and your observability telemetry cannot be in two separate data silos ... you will have to unify your telemetry because the assumption you have to make is the agent has already infiltrated your environment," Patel said.


"You have to prevent it at the policy layer. You have to prevent it at the at the application layer. You have to prevent it at every layer of the stack," he added.


*— Colleen McKown*

## Will AI agents have an "iPhone moment"?


watch now


VIDEO


3:33


03:33


When we may see AI agents' potential "iPhone moment"


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


As a society, we do not fully trust AI yet. For instance, most people are not giving AI access to their credit cards.


"There's something inside you that says, 'I can't trust this bot to not make purchases I don't want it to make,'" CNBC contributor Alex Kantrowitz said in a conversation on AI safety with Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel.


"I think if you look at society at large, the trust gap is pretty high right now. People don't trust these things to be able to use them, and for good reason," Patel said.


"I think we have to make sure that we get better at being able to constantly be able to monitor agent behavior, and then be able to intercept at runtime when agents are starting to show drift from human values and is misaligned with human values," he said.


Patel said he thinks there will be "meaningful progress" on this front over the next three to six months and predicts that personal agents will create a "catalytic moment, and it's going to happen sooner than you think."


"I think it'll be like the iPhone," he said, saying that his breakthrough in thinking came when an AI agent saved him $1,000 a year in subscriptions.


"That was the unlock for me. And so I do feel like there's an iPhone moment," Patel said.

## Keeping taste and judgment once AI is involved in creative decisions


Jason Gowans, Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer, speaks with CNBC's Jon Fortt at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026.


CNBC


Over the last year, Levi Strauss has deployed Stitch, an AI-powered super assistant designed to help store employees answer any question a customer may have as they shop for jeans or other items.


So as Levi's put this tool into the hands of thousands of workers across the globe, did it put as much effort into training workers to use it as it did to develop it?


Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer Jason Gowans said at the core of the company is a belief in "judgement and creativity," creating a "very fine line" when introducing a tool that is designed to increase productivity and efficiency while keeping that level of taste.


"The way we approach that from a training point of view is that we think about mindset, skill set and toolset," Gowans said.


An example of that, Gowans said, would be the concept of slow AI, which means to be "really intentional about when you get an output from AI, asking yourself what assumptions went into this output, where might there be biases, what evidence is missing from that answer?"


Gowans said a recent poll of employees suggested that the two things they most want to be trained in are critical thinking and strategic thinking.


"These are examples where we're teaching strategy formulation. We're teaching how to make decisions more effectively. That's firmly in the skill set side of the bucket," he said.

## How AI is helping Levi's sell jeans


watch now


VIDEO


5:29


05:29


Levi Strauss is using AI to help you find your next pair of jeans


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


AI is significantly changing the shopping experience, from product discovery to virtual fitting rooms. So, will an AI agent help you buy your next pair of jeans?


While Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer Jason Gowans told CNBC's Jon Fortt that he doesn't see AI agents doing that — "Maybe for some people, but I think buying denim is a fundamentally emotional experience," Gowans said — AI is informing how Levi's is improving the customer experience.


Last year, Levi's launched Stitch, an AI-powered tool for store staff, providing them with access to product details, inventory information, and operational information, all designed so that workers will always have an answer to a customer question.


"If you think about the world of denim, there are a lot of fits, there are a lot of questions around the type of denim," Gowans said. "But for a salesperson or a stylist, you may not know this, or you may not have the confidence yet to talk about these products … Stitch was a very simple idea, which was: how do I help every stylist be a world-class stylist and explain our products, and at the same time, minimize all the friction of the back of the house."


Gowans said that Levi's business is roughly 50% wholesale and 50% direct-to-consumer, and there is an "obsession about the customer experience" at the company to ensure shoppers are always satisfied.


When Stitch was rolled out, Gowans said it led to an eight-basis-point improvement in customer satisfaction in stores where it was being utilized.


"I've worked in retail for a very long time, and usually you're optimizing at the margins," he said. "So when you see an eight-point jump in customer satisfaction, where typically you might see a two- or three-point movement in a given year, that shows promise, and we want to lean in."

## Is there an entry-level AI usage paradox?


ADT Product Life Cycle Analyst Jemima Gay speaks with Sharon Epperson at CNBC's Technology Executive Council Summit on October 28, 2026 in New York City


CNBC


Many company leaders have been relying on entry-level employees coming in and being AI-literate. A CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit attendee asked early-level career professionals if they are seeing this among their teammates and how they have navigated the dichotomy with the education system generally trying to keep AI out.


"In school you're not learning how to use AI for business, so it's up to you to figure out the skills that you need to be AI fluent," said ADT Product Life Cycle Analyst Jemima Gay, who just graduated five months ago. "The companies are looking for entry-level workers, but more 'seniorized' skills, which you're not going to come out of school with."


Becoming AI fluent, Gay said, is something that workers need to spend a lot of time focusing on.


"I feel that unless you're in the tech space, you're not really building those skills as much as you should ... that's the contradiction there," she said.


Gay is also planning on going to graduate school to further study computer science. Epperson asked why she is choosing this path when AI is likely to take over many computer science jobs.


"I think that the work that we're doing now is not going to be replaced by AI; I definitely think AI is something that we're going to be working alongside," Gay said.


At the same time, Gay said, she is worried about the reduction in entry-level positions in general.


But, she said, "Being in the tech space and going to school for computer science I think is fitting because we're building the AI tools that we need to use in the workspace."


*— Colleen McKown*

## The AI cost debate


watch now


VIDEO


3:57


03:57


The current state of AI spending within companies


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


The shift from AI adoption to tokenmaxxing to AI cost restrictions has come quickly.


So, how are organizations thinking about AI costs right now?


Kiran Patel, WGSN chief technology officer and CNBC TEC Council member, said at the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit that at first, AI "was sort of like the rounding error in the technology budget."


"Now it's the second-largest line item after talent," Patel said.


While Patel said that has put AI usage under the microscope, it has not slowed down its usage. He pointed to recent Ramp data that suggests that AI costs at big companies has been largely flat in the last two months, even as usage has increased.


"That's the disciplines fitting in now, because they are going into the optimization phase," he said. "From experimentation to execution and now optimization."


However, he said, CFOs are now more focused on if this AI spend is leading to the intended outcomes. "If it's not, \[they're asking\] about replacing the existing vendor," he said.


David Treat, chief technology officer at Pearson, said this cycle has been seen before with other technology deployments.


"Pick your favorite scare resource that we get all fascinated about optimizing, and we go through a natural cycle of focusing on unit cost, Jevons Paradox kicks in, the unit cost goes down, the scale goes up, and then suddenly there's a big bill," Treat said. "My goal and focus with Pearson is can we get to the end faster and not having to go through the full cycle of having that CFO conversation be all about cost."


Treat said while it's always more difficult to measure an outcome than the cost input, "that's where we're putting our focus; less on the input and more on the output."


*— Ian Thomas*

## Hands-on learning is paramount with AI


watch now


VIDEO


3:52


03:52


Young workers on learning to use AI at work


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


AI trainings are becoming more common in many workplaces. CNBC's Sharon Epperson asked three early-career professionals how training has helped them in their roles.


"I think the most that I've learned about AI was through hands-on working with different types of projects, so helping my team minimize the amount of manual tasks that they have to do, or for creating status reports, for example," said ADT Product Life Cycle Analyst Jemima Gay.


Daniela Aizenman, Tenez AI strategist, agreed, saying that while she acknowledges the importance of companies providing AI training to their workers, there is no replacement for hands-on learning.


"I think some of the best training advice I ever got was from an old partner who was very AI-forward and always pushed the use of these tools," she said. "The only answer he ever gave me was just ask \[the AI tool\] Cursor."


"When you think of tools like Microsoft Word or Excel, you probably got a one end-to-end training where you learned functionality that still serves you today. But with tools like Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, features are being constantly rolled out, and so I think one of the best ways to upskill and continue training you and your teammates is to just ask the tool and get comfortable self-teaching yourself how to best use it in your day to day," Aizenman said.

## Keeping the human in content creation to avoid 'AI slop'


Three young professionals speak with CNBC's Sharon Epperson at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit on October 28, 2026. about how they are utilizing AI in their roles.


CNBC


As AI becomes more common in the workplace and in content online and on social media, the conversation around "AI slop," or low-quality content produced with little human oversight, has intensified.


CNBC's Sharon Epperson talked with three early-career professionals about how they navigate issues around AI slop and keeping the human element in AI-produced content.


"I think it's really important to not only have context but also feed the tool what good looks like. At the end of the day, we're all amazing at our jobs and we've done this without AI," Daniela Aizenman, AI strategist at Tenez, said.


Orlando Foods Brand & Engagement Specialist Ally Figliuolo agreed, saying, "I completely relate to Daniela about prompting it in the best way you can and giving it the best information."


"I think the most important thing is always still relating it back to a human connection," Figliuolo said. "I really do read through every single detail, and it does take a little bit more time."


*— Colleen McKown*

## The New York Liberty’s AI “championship moment”


Keia Cole, Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment Chief Digital Officer, speaks with CNBC's Scott Wapner at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 28, 2026.


CNBC


Keia Cole, the chief digital officer of Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, recalled the excitement of the New York Liberty's first WNBA title in 2004 at the 2026 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit.


But there was another off-court moment Cole said ranks up there during her tenure with the organization: a company-wide AI lab launched earlier this year.


"We were trying to figure out how to increase AI fluency across the organization, and we were doing the typical things: training, office hours, and meeting with specific departments," Cole told CNBC's Scott Wapner. "It wasn't getting us where we needed to go."


Cole said the strategy needed to shift, and a decision was made to encourage certain AI behaviors.


That led to the launch of an internal AI lab, an eight-week program that started on the literal basis of how you even identify a problem that AI can solve. From there, the program was scaled up, moving from identification to prototypes to solutions.


"It was the equivalent of a science fair," Cole said, adding that the organization ended up with 14 solutions that spanned from fan engagement to budgeting to internal mentorship tools.


"There were a lot of ambitious efforts, and I was surprised at the complexity of the problems that people wanted to solve," she said. "We also saw a lot of cross-functional teams and people seeking out others or teams that maybe they wouldn't have worked with before."


Cole said that while there were winners (and those that won received cash prizes), now the program is live all the time, allowing employees to think up new solutions for problems they encounter.


"There's a real belief in our organization that if you create value for the organization, we will return some of that value to you," Cole said.

## AI personalization is the next wave of sports fan engagement


watch now


VIDEO


4:51


04:51


How the Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty are using AI to better connect with fans


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


Owned by Alibaba Group Chairperson Joseph Tsai, Brooklyn Sports and Entertainment has always looked to leverage technology across the Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty, as well as within the Barclays Center where the two teams play.


Keia Cole, chief digital officer at Brooklyn Sports and Entertainment, told CNBC's Scott Wapner that the organization has looked to dive even further into AI after seeing what it could do to elevate the fan experience.


"The core product, you're not going to disrupt," Cole said. "There's still going to be humans on the basketball court. There's still going to be artists coming to do concerts … but we really have this opportunity to think differently about how we work, how we serve our customers, and how we serve our fans, and get better content to them more efficiently, make it faster for them to get to where they're going in the building and have more knowledge about that."


Cole said that those are the things that "power the experience to make it feel like, 'Yeah, I want to get off my couch and come to an arena.'"


That has meant using AI to improve the teams' existing applications, help personalize the touchpoints that each fan has with the organization, and ticketing, among other things.


"How do we understand our fans and communicate to them in a way that's personalized?" Cole said. "If you think about the nature of fandom, people are very dedicated, they're very committed … we have all this detail for what it means to show up as a fan, and I think we should be giving that same attention to detail and commitment back to the fans — using AI and personalization is one way to do that."

## Should AI agents be treated as employees?


Mason Argiropoulos, Paychex CHRO, and Barbra Katz, Crum & Forster CHRO, spoke with CNBC's Susan Caminiti at CNBC's Technology Executive Council Summit on October 28, 2026 in New York City.


CNBC


AI agents are starting to outnumber human employees at some companies. Should they also be considered employees?


A question from the CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit crowd posed that question to Paychex CHRO Mason Argiropoulos and Crum & Forster CHRO Barbra Katz, wondering how they are thinking about this. Do you have to think about treating non-human agent workers the way you treat humans, and maybe they will behave better if you do that?, the question asked.


Argiropoulos, a CNBC Workforce Executive Council member, said he and fellow WEC and Technology Executive Council members were actually discussing this at dinner last night, asking questions like whether agents should get performance reviews.


"At our company, we've got thousands of agents that are doing work of all different kinds. We haven't yet integrated that into a lot of our people management processes just yet," he said.


Argiropoulos acknowledged that agents need a degree of coaching and performance management. "You have to monitor what they're doing, and if they're not doing what they're supposed to be doing, then you need to try to give them some additional prompting or some additional guidance so that they can ultimately achieve the result that you want to," he said. "But I think we are still early days."


Katz, also a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, said, "\[There are\] no agents on the org chart for me. That's not something that I envision happening, and I think that's dangerous territory."


While agents do have to be trained, she said "We shouldn't confuse that with a human or human behavior."

## Are open-weight models the future of AI?


watch now


VIDEO


5:43


05:43


The evolution happening in AI architecture


[Technology Executive Council](https://www.cnbc.com/tec/)


There is plenty of debate around which AI firm will be at the top of the mountain as the technology continues to be deployed across the economy and society.


But from the perspective of Calix CEO Michael Weening, for companies like his that are using those models to deliver platforms to customers, it's critical that organizations design their systems to be ready for any future.


"If we keep all the things that are valuable, which is we have the knowledge, we have all the workflows, we have the trust and security … as they commoditize, we can actually just flip the open-weight model out and put a new one in, and just keep flipping them in and out as these guys go to war," Weening said. "We're going to go take the best of the best at all times."


Weening said he is increasingly betting that the future is based in open-weight models after what he said would be a "mass commoditization" of AI.


"We firmly believe that you're going to see a mass commoditization, and that there is no value in AI because these are self-learning systems, and therefore they're going to be commodities," he said. "We wanted to be able to take advantage of what's the best commodity on the market today."


Calix Chief Product Officer Shane Eleniak said it's becoming clear that the problems that the company is trying to solve, like many other companies, won't be solved "with a generalist, centralized approach. It's going to need to be specialized."


"You just look at the scale of the problem. It's no different than saying, why do we have brain surgeons and car mechanics? They're very, very different skill sets. You start looking at security. You start looking at some of the bigger distributed problems. You're not going to solve that with the centralized approach," he said.
